text: Peyton Farquhar, a wealthy planter from an old Alabama family, was a slave owner who strongly supported the Southern side in the war. <break time="0.8s" /> Unable to join the army for reasons he could not control, he longed for a chance to do something brave for the South. <break time="0.8s" /> One evening, while Farquhar and his wife were sitting on a bench near the gate, a soldier in a gray uniform rode up to them. <break time="0.8s" /> Missus Farquhar was glad to bring him a cup of water, and while she was gone, her husband eagerly asked for news from the front. <break time="0.8s" /> The soldier said that the Northern army had reached the Owl Creek bridge, where they were repairing the railroad and had built a small fort. <break time="0.8s" /> Any civilian caught damaging the railroad or its bridges will be hanged, he added, and I have seen the order myself. <break time="0.8s" /> Smiling, Farquhar asked what a brave man could do there if he managed to get past the guard at the end of the bridge. <break time="0.8s" /> The soldier answered that a great pile of dry driftwood lay against the wooden pier, and that it would burn very easily. <break time="0.8s" /> Later that night the soldier rode back past the plantation in the opposite direction, for he was really a Northern scout in disguise.
